headline: New Hampshire high court leaves state’s lone death sentence intact
dek: The justices dismissed Michael Addison’s latest petition for another proportionality review, but the ruling does not schedule an execution or resolve a separate constitutional challenge.
body: The New Hampshire Supreme Court on Tuesday dismissed Michael Addison’s latest effort to overturn his death sentence, leaving the state’s only capital punishment case in place while other legal questions remain unresolved. The court’s opinion in [Petition of Addison](https://www.leagle.com/decision/innhco20261006459), issued Oct. 6, said state law does not authorize a second comparative proportionality review of a capital sentence that the court already examined.

Addison, now 46, has spent roughly two decades in prison for the 2006 killing of Manchester police Officer Michael Briggs. A jury convicted him of capital murder and sentenced him to death in 2008. The New Hampshire Bulletin reported that Addison’s sentence was the last death sentence imposed before lawmakers repealed capital punishment in 2019. The repeal was written to apply prospectively, leaving Addison’s sentence as the exception that has continued to test the state’s courts and political system.

The petition focused on whether the court should revisit the proportionality of Addison’s punishment after that repeal. His lawyers and the American Civil Liberties Union of New Hampshire argued that the state should not be able to execute one person while the death penalty is unavailable for everyone convicted later. They also raised concerns about racial disparity, pointing to other New Hampshire murder cases in which defendants received life without parole. The [New Hampshire Bulletin](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/06/nh-supreme-court-denies-death-row-inmates-latest-appeal/) described those arguments as part of the case presented to the justices.

The court did not decide that a new comparison would be unfavorable to Addison. Instead, Justice Melissa Countway wrote that the legislature had not given the court authority to conduct successive reviews. The justices had already concluded in 2015 that Addison’s sentence was neither excessive nor disproportionate, according to the [Boston Globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/06/metro/new-hampshire-supreme-court-dismisses-michael-addison-appeal/). Because the statute did not expressly create another review after repeal, the court dismissed the petition rather than reopening that analysis.

That distinction matters for what Tuesday’s order does—and does not—mean. The ruling keeps the death sentence legally operative for now, but it does not set a date for an execution. Addison’s attorneys told the Globe that another case challenging the constitutionality of his death sentence is still pending, leaving a separate route for further litigation. The decision also does not revisit the jury’s 2008 verdict or change the sentence for any other person incarcerated in New Hampshire.

The case remains closely tied to Manchester and to the Briggs family. Briggs was 35 when he was fatally shot while responding to a reported gunshot during an overnight domestic incident, the Globe reported. The killing prompted lasting mourning among Manchester officers and residents. One of Briggs’s sons later entered law enforcement and served as police chief in Grafton, giving the case an enduring connection to the region’s public-safety community.

The ruling also keeps capital punishment in the center of New Hampshire’s 2026 political debate. Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who prosecuted Addison as attorney general, said the court’s decision was an important step toward justice for Briggs and his family. Democratic challenger Cinde Warmington has said she would not pursue the death-penalty aspect of Addison’s sentence if elected governor, according to the Globe. The competing positions show why a case involving one prisoner continues to matter statewide: it tests the meaning of a repeal law, the reach of judicial review and the role of the governor in a sentence that the state no longer imposes on new defendants.

For now, the confirmed legal position is narrower than either side’s preferred outcome. New Hampshire’s high court has declined to conduct another proportionality review, Addison remains the only person on death row in New England, and his attorneys retain other avenues to challenge the sentence. Any future change would have to come through those proceedings, a new ruling, or action by the state’s political branches—not from Tuesday’s dismissal alone.
